items.title: Type-A Hecke Specht modules are in the same block iff their labels have the same e-core
items.statement:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), and let $S^{\lambda}$ be the type-A Hecke Specht module of this page in the Dipper-James convention ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) for $\lambda\vdash n$. Then for all partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ the modules $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Equivalently, for finite $e$, the blocks of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ of size at most $n$ with $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. For $e=\infty$ use $C_\infty(\lambda):=\lambda$; the Hecke algebra is semisimple and its blocks are indexed by partitions of $n$.

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$, an integer $n\ge0$, the Hecke algebra $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ with Specht modules $S^{\lambda}$ for $\lambda\vdash n$, and a fixed integer $d\ge n$.

[F1] For $d\ge n$, the Schur idempotent $e\in S=S_F(d,n)$ satisfies $eSe\cong H$, and $X\mapsto Xe$ is exact. It sends each Weyl module $W^{\lambda}$ to the nonzero Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$; its simple images are zero or the Murphy simple modules, with the nonzero images indexed by the $e$-restricted partitions ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F2] Blocks: $1=\sum_D\delta_D$ is the unique decomposition of the identity of a finite-dimensional algebra into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents, blocks are the ideals cut out by the $\delta_D$, and every nonzero central idempotent is a sum of some of the $\delta_D$ ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]).

[F3] The q-Schur algebra and its Weyl modules: $S$ is finite-dimensional, $S=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for $M=\bigoplus_{\nu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\nu}$ with $M^{(1^n)}=H$, and $W^{\lambda}_F$ has head $L^{\lambda}_F$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

[F4] The q-Schur block theorem [[thm-q-schur-weyl-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]]: for $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F,W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S$ if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$; the blocks of $S$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$, $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$; and if $e=\infty$ then $S$ is semisimple with each $W^{\lambda}_F$ its own block.

[F5] The accepted ordinary/Murphy dictionary identifies the ordinary Specht module with the fixed $\theta$ pullback of the conjugate-shape Murphy cell module. Conjugation sends $C_e(\lambda)$ to $C_e(\lambda)'$, and sends restricted labels to regular labels. In particular it preserves equality of cores. An algebra automorphism permutes primitive central idempotents and therefore preserves the same-block relation ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Central idempotents of $H$ from blocks of $S$. For a block $C$ of $S$ with primitive central idempotent $\epsilon_C$ put $\tilde\epsilon_C:=\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Ce\in H$. This element is a central idempotent of $H$: it is idempotent because $\epsilon_C$ is, and for $x=ese\in H$ centrality of $\epsilon_C$ gives $x\tilde\epsilon_C=es\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Cse=\tilde\epsilon_Cx$; it is nonzero because it acts as the identity on the nonzero module $W^{\lambda}_Fe=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ for any $\lambda$ with $W^{\lambda}_F\in C$, namely $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\tilde\epsilon_C=W^{\lambda}_Fe\epsilon_Ce=W^{\lambda}_F\epsilon_Ce=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. Moreover $\tilde\epsilon_C\tilde\epsilon_{C'}=e\epsilon_C\epsilon_{C'}e=0$ for $C\ne C'$ and $\sum_C\tilde\epsilon_C=e\sum_C\epsilon_Ce=e^2=1_H$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Number of q-Schur blocks is at least the number of Hecke blocks. Let $H=\bigoplus_iB_i$ be the block decomposition of $H$ with block identities $b_i$. Since $M=\bigoplus_{\nu}M^{\nu}$ and $H=M^{(1^n)}$ is a direct summand, $M=\bigoplus_iMb_i$ with each $Mb_i\ne0$ (it contains $Hb_i=B_i$), and $\mathrm{Hom}_H(Mb_i,Mb_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$, because a map $f$ satisfies $f(x)=f(xb_i)=f(x)b_i\in Mb_jb_i=0$. Hence $$S=\mathrm{End}_H(M)=\bigoplus_{i,j}\mathrm{Hom}_H(Mb_i,Mb_j)=\prod_i\mathrm{End}_H(Mb_i)$$ is a product of the nonzero algebras $\mathrm{End}_H(Mb_i)$, and a product of nonzero algebras has at least one block per factor; so $\#\{\text{blocks of }S\}\ge\#\{\text{blocks of }H\}$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Number of Hecke blocks is at least the number of q-Schur blocks. Decompose each nonzero central idempotent $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 into primitive central idempotents of $H$ using the unique decomposition of $1_H$: every primitive central idempotent $\delta_D$ of $H$ with $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C=\delta_D$ belongs to exactly one $\tilde\epsilon_C$, because $\delta_D=\delta_D\cdot1_H=\sum_C\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C$ and pairwise orthogonality of the $\delta_D$ forces $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C\in\{0,\delta_D\}$. Since each $\tilde\epsilon_C\ne0$ has at least one such $\delta_D$, the blocks $D$ of $H$ are partitioned into nonempty supports over the blocks $C$ of $S$, and therefore $\#\{\text{blocks of }H\}\ge\#\{\text{blocks of }S\}$. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 A bijection of block sets, and the core criterion. By steps 2.1 and 1.2 the two block counts are equal, so each $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 has exactly one primitive summand and the map $C\mapsto\tilde\epsilon_C$ is a bijection from the blocks of $S$ onto the blocks of $H$. Since $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\lambda}_Fe$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\mu}_Fe$, the modules $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}$ lie in the same Hecke block if and only if $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same q-Schur block: indeed the block of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the image under the bijection of the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$. By the block theorem [F4] the latter holds if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$, which proves the q-Schur-normalised statement. [F1, F4, step 2.1, step 1.2]

4.1 Ordinary normalisation and semisimplicity. By [F5], $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block exactly when $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}$ do. Step 3.1 makes this equivalent to $C_e(\lambda')=C_e(\mu')$, and the identity $C_e(\nu')=C_e(\nu)'$ makes it equivalent to $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$. This identity follows by conjugating every removable border strip in a core-removal sequence; the terminal core also conjugates, by independence of removal order. For $e=\infty$, $S$ is semisimple by [F4]. Its corner $eSe$ is semisimple: by [[thm-wedderburn-artin-theorem]], in the Wedderburn decomposition of $S$, each idempotent selects a subspace in each matrix factor, and its corner is a product of matrix algebras over the same division rings. Thus $H\cong eSe$ is semisimple; the block bijection separates the partition labels. This proves all assertions. [F1, F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

items.title: Nakayama block classification for symmetric groups
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a splitting field of characteristic $p>0$ (equivalently the residue field of the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, [[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]], [[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]) and let $n\ge0$. Two Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k,S^{\mu}_k$ of $k[S_n]$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ have the same $p$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Consequently the blocks of $k[S_n]$ are indexed by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $\gamma$ a $p$-core, $w\in\mathbb N_0$ and $n=|\gamma|+pw$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$ with $w_p(\lambda)=(n-|C_p(\lambda)|)/p$ ([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A splitting field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$ with the fixed splitting $p$-modular system, an integer $n\ge0$, and the group algebra $k[S_n]$ with group Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k$ for $\lambda\vdash n$.

[F1] The algebra isomorphism $H_{k,1}(S_n)\cong k[S_n]$ sends each ordinary Dipper-James Specht module to the classical group Specht module of the same shape, and the quantum characteristic at $q=1$ in characteristic $p$ equals $p$ ([[prop-hecke-specht-theory-specializes-to-group-specht-theory-at-q-one]], [[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]). The module comparison uses the accepted signed conjugate Murphy/ordinary dictionary before specialising; it does not identify the same-shape Murphy cell module with the ordinary Specht module.

[F2] The Hecke block criterion, in the Dipper-James normalisation of the same Specht modules as [F1]: [[cor-type-a-hecke-specht-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]] states that for a field $k$ and $q\in k^{\times}$ of quantum characteristic $e\ge2$, two Specht modules $S^{\lambda},S^{\mu}$ of $H_{k,q}(S_n)$ lie in the same block if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$, and that the blocks are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$.

[F4] The core-quotient size formula [[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]: for every $e\ge2$ and $\lambda\vdash n$ one has $n=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda)$ with $w_e(\lambda)=|Q_e(\lambda)|\in\mathbb N_0$, and for an $e$-core $\gamma$ the condition $|\gamma|\le n$, $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$ is exactly the condition that $n-|\gamma|$ be an admissible $e$-weight; conversely every such $\gamma$ occurs as the core of a partition of $n$ ([[thm-q-schur-weyl-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]).

[F5] An algebra isomorphism $\varphi:A\to B$ preserves blocks: it maps a central idempotent $z$ to the central idempotent $\varphi(z)$, preserves primitivity, and hence induces a bijection between the block sets ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Specialisation. Take $q=1\in k^{\times}$ and $e$ the quantum characteristic of $(k,q)$; since $q=1$ and $\operatorname{char}k=p>0$, [F1] gives $e=p$. By [F1] there is an algebra isomorphism $H_{k,1}(S_n)\cong k[S_n]$ carrying the Hecke Specht modules of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$ to the group Specht modules $S^{\lambda}_k$, so by [F5] this isomorphism induces a bijection between the blocks of the two algebras that matches $S^{\lambda}$ with $S^{\lambda}_k$; in particular $S^{\lambda}_k$ and $S^{\mu}_k$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if the corresponding Hecke Specht modules lie in the same block of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$. [F1, F5, algebra]

2.1 The core criterion. Applying the Hecke block criterion [F2] with $q=1$ and $e=p$, the Hecke Specht modules of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$ lie in the same block if and only if the labels $\lambda,\mu$ have the same $p$-core. Together with step 1.1 this gives: $S^{\lambda}_k$ and $S^{\mu}_k$ lie in the same block of $k[S_n]$ if and only if $C_p(\lambda)=C_p(\mu)$. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 The parametrisation by cores and weights. By [F2] the blocks of $H_{k,1}(S_n)$, hence by step 1.1 the blocks of $k[S_n]$, are indexed by the $p$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$ and $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod p$; the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ corresponds to $C_p(\lambda)$. For $n\ge0$ and such a $\gamma$ put $w:=(n-|\gamma|)/p\in\mathbb N_0$; by [F4] this is exactly the $p$-weight $w_p(\lambda)$ of any Specht label with core $\gamma$, and $n=|\gamma|+pw$. Since $w$ is determined by $n$ and $\gamma$, the map $\gamma\mapsto(\gamma,w)$ is a bijection onto the displayed set of pairs, and the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ is the pair $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$. [F4, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Steps 2.1 and 3.1 establish both assertions: the same-block criterion by the $p$-core, and the indexing of the blocks by the pairs $(\gamma,w)$ with $n=|\gamma|+pw$ together with the identification of the block of $S^{\lambda}_k$ as $(C_p(\lambda),w_p(\lambda))$. [step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

The classification is stated independently, by a Young-module and Brauer-quotient route, as Theorem 1 of O'Donovan's preprint recorded in the sources; that reference is an independent confirmation of the statement and is not used in the proof above. No choice principle is used anywhere in this item.

items.title: Weight-zero symmetric-group blocks are defect zero
items.statement:
Let $k$ be a splitting field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$
be a partition of $p$-weight $w_p(\lambda)=0$, that is, a $p$-core
([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Then the block $B$ of $k[S_n]$
containing $S^{\lambda}_k$
([[thm-nakayama-block-classification-for-symmetric-groups]]) contains exactly
one Specht label, namely $\lambda$; its decomposition matrix is the $1\times1$
matrix $(1)$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is both the unique simple and the unique
projective indecomposable module of $B$; its Cartan matrix is $(1)$; the
block algebra is a full matrix algebra over $k$; and $B$ has trivial defect
group, that is, defect zero in the fixed splitting modular system
([[def-defect-group-and-numerical-defect-of-a-block]]).

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A splitting field $k$ of characteristic $p>0$ for $S_n$ and all its subgroups, an integer $n\ge0$, a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ with $w_p(\lambda)=0$, and the block $B$ of $k[S_n]$ containing $S^{\lambda}_k$.

[F1] $w_p(\lambda)=(n-|C_p(\lambda)|)/p$, so $w_p(\lambda)=0$ is equivalent to $C_p(\lambda)=\lambda$, and a $p$-core is $p$-regular ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]). Hence $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ and $S^{\lambda}_k$ has simple head $D^{\lambda}$, with $D^{\lambda}$ its unique maximal quotient, so $S^{\lambda}_k$ is indecomposable ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]).

[F2] Nakayama: two Specht modules of $k[S_n]$ lie in the same block if and only if their labels have the same $p$-core ([[thm-nakayama-block-classification-for-symmetric-groups]]); the blocks are indexed by the $p$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$, $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod p$. The simple $k[S_n]$-modules are exactly the $D^{\mu}$ for the $p$-regular $\mu\vdash n$, pairwise non-isomorphic ([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]).

[F3] Block bookkeeping: the identity of $k[S_n]$ decomposes uniquely into primitive central idempotents, every finite-dimensional module decomposes along the blocks, and a simple module lies in exactly one block ([[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]); in particular an indecomposable finite-dimensional module lies in a single block.

[F4] Dominance unitriangularity: $d_{\mu\mu}=1$ and $d_{\mu\nu}\ne0$ implies $\nu\unrhd\mu$ for the modular decomposition numbers $d_{\mu\nu}=[S^{\mu}_k:D^{\nu}]$ ([[thm-symmetric-group-decomposition-matrix-is-dominance-unitriangular]]).

[F5] For a block $B$ with decomposition matrix $D_B$ and Cartan matrix $C_B$ one has $C_B=D_B^{\mathsf T}D_B$ ([[thm-cartan-matrix-is-d-transpose-d]]); the $(1,1)$-entry of $C_B$ is the multiplicity of the simple module in its projective cover ([[def-projective-indecomposable-characters-and-cartan-invariants]]).

[F6] Defect-zero criterion: over the splitting residue field, for a block $B$ the following are equivalent: the defect group of $B$ is trivial; $B$ is a full matrix algebra over $k$; $B$ has a projective simple module; in that case there is exactly one simple module and it is projective ([[thm-defect-zero-blocks-are-simple-algebras]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Bookkeeping for the labels of $B$. Let $\nu\vdash n$ be a $p$-regular partition with block $B(\nu)=B$; by [F1] and [F2] this is equivalent to $C_p(\nu)=C_p(\lambda)=\lambda$, and since $|\nu|=n=|\lambda|$ this forces $\nu=\lambda$. Hence the only $p$-regular label in $B$ is $\lambda$, and by [F2] the only simple module in $B$ is $D^{\lambda}$. For any Specht label $\mu$ in $B$, [F2] gives $C_p(\mu)=\lambda$ and $|\mu|=|\lambda|$, so $\mu=\lambda$ as well: the block has exactly one Specht row. Since $S^{\lambda}_k$ is indecomposable with head $D^{\lambda}$ by [F1] and lies in $B$ by hypothesis, the decomposition matrix of $B$ is the $1\times1$ matrix with entry $d_{\lambda\lambda}=[S^{\lambda}_k:D^{\lambda}]=1$, by the exact diagonal multiplicity in [F4]. A simple head alone would not establish multiplicity one. [F1, F2, F3, F4]

2.1 The Cartan matrix and the projective cover. By [F5] applied to the block $B$ the Cartan matrix of $B$ is $C_B=D_B^{\mathsf T}D_B=(1)$, so the projective cover $P^{\lambda}$ of $D^{\lambda}$ has $D^{\lambda}$ as its only composition factor, with multiplicity one. A nonzero module of length one is simple, so $P^{\lambda}\cong D^{\lambda}$: the block $B$ has a projective simple module. [F1, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Defect zero and the matrix algebra. By step 2.1 the projective indecomposable $P^{\lambda}$ equals the simple $D^{\lambda}$, and it is the unique projective indecomposable of $B$ because the simple modules of $B$ are in bijection with its projective indecomposables; so $D^{\lambda}$ is both the unique simple and the unique projective indecomposable of $B$. The defect-zero criterion [F6] now gives that $B$ is a full matrix algebra over $k$ and that the defect group of $B$ is trivial, that is, $B$ has defect zero in the fixed splitting modular system. [F5, F6, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Steps 1.1, 2.1 and 3.1 give all the assertions: the single Specht label $\lambda$, the decomposition matrix $(1)$, the unique simple and projective indecomposable $D^{\lambda}$, the Cartan matrix $(1)$, the full matrix algebra structure and defect zero. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

items.title: Block weight is not the same as numerical defect
items.statement:
**Weight is combinatorial.** The $e$-weight $w_e(\lambda)$ of a label is the
number of $e$-hooks that have to be removed from $\lambda$ to reach its
$e$-core, it equals the size $|Q_e(\lambda)|$ of the $e$-quotient, and it
satisfies $n=|\lambda|=|C_e(\lambda)|+e\,w_e(\lambda)$
([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]). In particular
$w_e(\lambda)$ is determined by the $e$-core, so by [[cor-type-a-hecke-specht-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]]
it is an invariant of the block of $S^{\lambda}$; for $e=p$ it is the
combinatorial $p$-weight of the block.

**Numerical defect is block-theoretic.** The numerical defect of a block is
defined from its defect group: for the block bimodule $kGb$ a defect group is
a $p$-subgroup $D\le G$ for which the diagonal $\Delta D$ is a vertex, its
order $p^d$ defines the numerical defect $d$, and defect zero means $D=1$
([[def-defect-group-and-numerical-defect-of-a-block]]). It is a $p$-adic order
invariant of the block algebra in the fixed splitting modular system and is
defined by a vertex computation, not by hook combinatorics.

**The two invariants must not be identified without a theorem and an explicit
range.** The weight records how many hooks of length divisible by $e$ the
label carries, while the numerical defect records the order of a vertex of the
block bimodule; nothing on this page proves that the two numbers agree, and
they are defined from entirely different data. The only case settled here is
weight zero: if $w_p(\lambda)=0$ then $\lambda$ is a $p$-core, and the
classification forces the block to have a single Specht label, Cartan matrix
$(1)$, a projective simple module, a full matrix algebra structure and trivial
defect group, so the numerical defect is also zero
([[prop-weight-zero-symmetric-group-blocks-are-defect-zero]]). For $w>0$ no
assertion about the defect group of a weight-$w$ symmetric-group block, and no
identification of $w$ with the numerical defect, is made on this page. The
printed defect-group computation for weight-$w$ blocks (defect $\nu_p((pw)!)$,
with defect group a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $S_{pw}$) is deliberately not
asserted here, because no counted proof source for it is registered with this
batch; supplying it is outside this page's proof route and remains an open
obligation for a later page of the track.

No choice principle is used in the statements recorded above.
items.strategy: The core/quotient size and hook count definitions are distinguished correctly from the vertex order defining numerical defect. At fixed rank and finite e, block-weight invariance uses precisely the Hecke core classification; weight-zero defect uses the exact preceding proposition. No positive-weight defect-group formula is asserted as a theorem, and no equality of the invariants is inferred. Read all four actual suppliers; reader added the missing Hecke-block dependency. That cited classification and weight-zero consequence are still held on the batch-13 Schur foundation, so this complete current remark cannot be accepted unconditionally. Owner must resolve the two missing constructions; risk remains open.

title: Cores, Quotients, and Blocks of Symmetric Groups — Examples

items.title: The three-core and three-quotient of (6,5,2,1^3) by abacus
items.statement:
Work with $e=3$ and $\lambda=(6,5,2,1^3)\vdash16$, whose $\beta$-set is
$X_\lambda=\{11,9,5,3,2,1\}$
([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). On the $3$-abacus the
beads sit on runners $0,1,2$ at positions $9,3$ on runner $0$, $1$ on runner
$1$ and $11,5,2$ on runner $2$. Top-packing every runner gives the core beads
$3,0$ on runner $0$, $1$ on runner $1$ and $8,5,2$ on runner $2$, so
$C_3(\lambda)=(3,1)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]); with the
normalising condition $3\mid|X|=6$ the runner row-label sets are
$X^{(3)}_0=\{3,1\}$, $X^{(3)}_1=\{0\}$ and $X^{(3)}_2=\{3,1,0\}$, giving the
quotient $Q_3(\lambda)=((2,1),\varnothing,(1))$. Four bead moves are required,
and the size formula
$$16=|(3,1)|+3\,(|(2,1)|+|\varnothing|+|(1)|)=4+3\cdot4$$
holds ([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]); the same-runner
bead-gap pairs realise the corresponding rim $3$-hook removals
([[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]],
[[thm-e-quotient-controls-hooks-divisible-by-e]],
[[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]).

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $e=3$, the partition $\lambda=(6,5,2,1^3)$ of $16$ with
$\beta$-set $X=X_\lambda=\{11,9,5,3,2,1\}$, and the $3$-abacus positions
$3a+i$ of runner $i$ and row $a$
([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]).

[F1] A $\beta$-set and its partition are related by
$P(\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\})=(h_1-(m-1),\dots,h_m-0)$ with trailing zeros deleted;
the elements of $X_\lambda$ are the first-column hook lengths
$b_i(\lambda)=\lambda_i+\ell(\lambda)-i$
([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]).

[F2] The hooks of a partition with $\beta$-set $Y$ correspond bijectively to
the bead-gap pairs $(b,g)$ of $Y$, i.e. $b\in Y$, $g\notin Y$, $0\le g<b$, the
corresponding hook having length $b-g$; the hook has length divisible by $3$
exactly when $b\equiv g\pmod3$; and removing it replaces $Y$ by
$(Y\setminus\{b\})\cup\{g\}$
([[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]]).

[F3] On the $3$-abacus the row-label set of runner $i$ is
$Y^{(3)}_i=\{a:3a+i\in Y\}$, the top-packed set is
$Y^{(3)}=\bigcup_{i=0}^{2}\{3a+i:0\le a\le|Y^{(3)}_i|-1\}$, the $3$-core is
$C_3(\cdot)=P(Y^{(3)})$, and for a normalised $\beta$-set with $3\mid|Y|$ the
$3$-quotient components are $\lambda^{(i)}=P(Y^{(3)}_i)$ with weight
$w_3=|Q_3|=\sum_i|\lambda^{(i)}|$
([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]).

[F4] $C_3(\lambda)$ is the terminal partition of every maximal sequence of
removals of removable border strips of size $3$, and $|\lambda\setminus R|=
|\lambda|-3$ for each such strip $R$
([[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]).

[F5] There is a bijection $f$ from the hooks of $\lambda$ of $3$-divisible
length onto the hooks of $Q_3(\lambda)$ with $|H|=3\,|f(H)|$ and
$Q_3(\lambda\setminus H)=Q_3(\lambda)\setminus f(H)$
([[thm-e-quotient-controls-hooks-divisible-by-e]]); and
$16=|\lambda|=|C_3(\lambda)|+3\,w_3(\lambda)$ with $w_3(\lambda)$ the number
of such hooks ([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Beads on the runners: reading positions $3a+i$ of $X=\{11,9,5,3,2,1\}$ gives runner $0$ the positions $9=3\cdot3$, $3=3\cdot1$, runner $1$ the position $1=3\cdot0+1$, and runner $2$ the positions $11=3\cdot3+2$, $5=3\cdot1+2$, $2=3\cdot0+2$. Hence the row-label sets are $X^{(3)}_0=\{3,1\}$, $X^{(3)}_1=\{0\}$, $X^{(3)}_2=\{3,1,0\}$, of counts $2,1,3$. [given, F1, F3]

1.2 Top-packing moves the two beads of runner $0$ to rows $0,1$, the bead of runner $1$ to row $0$, and the three beads of runner $2$ to rows $0,1,2$, so $$X^{(3)}=\{0,3\}\cup\{1\}\cup\{2,5,8\}=\{8,5,3,2,1,0\}$$ and, by [F1] with the six beads listed in decreasing order, $$C_3(\lambda)=P(X^{(3)})=(8-5,\,5-4,\,3-3,\,2-2,\,1-1,\,0-0)=(3,1).$$ [given, F1, F3]

2.1 The normalisation $3\mid|X|=6$ holds, so the row-label sets of step 1.1 may be read as $1$-abaci: $\lambda^{(0)}=P(\{3,1\})=(2,1)$, $\lambda^{(1)}=P(\{0\})=\varnothing$ and $\lambda^{(2)}=P(\{3,1,0\})=(1)$, so $Q_3(\lambda)=((2,1),\varnothing,(1))$ and $w_3(\lambda)=2+1+0+1=4$. [given, F1, F3, step 1.1]

2.2 Four upward bead moves lead from $X$ to $X^{(3)}$: $11\mapsto8$ on runner $2$ (the target $8\notin X$), then $9\mapsto6$ on runner $0$ ($6\notin X$), then $3\mapsto0$ on runner $0$ ($0\notin X$), then $6\mapsto3$ on runner $0$ (now $3\notin X$); every move replaces a bead by a gap one row above it on its own runner, so by [F2] each is the removal of a rim hook of length $3$. In terms of [F1] the intermediate partitions are $$(6,5,2,1^3)\to(4,4,2,1^3)\to(3,2,2,1^3)\to(3,2,2)\to(3,1),$$ each step of size $3$ by [F4], and the terminal partition is $C_3(\lambda)=(3,1)$ as computed in step 1.2. [given, F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, construct]

3.1 The size formula of [F5] reads $16=|C_3(\lambda)|+3\,w_3(\lambda)=4+3\cdot4$, using steps 1.2 and 2.1; the fourth move of step 2.2 is the last of the $w_3(\lambda)=4$ removals of size $3$ exhibited there. The four hooks of $\lambda$ of $3$-divisible length, read from the hook-length diagram (rows $11,7,5,4,3,1$; $9,5,3,2,1$; $5,1$; $3$; $2$; $1$), are $H_{1,5}$ of length $3$, $H_{2,1}$ of length $9$, $H_{2,3}$ of length $3$ and $H_{4,1}$ of length $3$, and the bijection $f$ of [F5] sends them to the hooks $H_{1,1}(\lambda^{(2)})$, $H_{1,1}(\lambda^{(0)})$, $H_{1,2}(\lambda^{(0)})$, $H_{2,1}(\lambda^{(0)})$ of sizes $1,3,1,1$ of $(1)$, $(2,1)$, matching $|H|=3|f(H)|$ in each case; all assertions of the Example are thereby checked. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

items.title: The three-core of (4,3,2,1) by two removal orders
items.statement:
Let $e=3$ and $\lambda=(4,3,2,1)\vdash10$, with $\beta$-set
$X=\{7,5,3,1\}$ ([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]). Two
different orders of removing rim $3$-hooks both terminate at the $3$-core
$(1)$, in agreement with the order-independence theorem
([[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]): on the
$3$-abacus the beads $7,5,3,1$ lie on runners $1,2,0,1$, and sliding beads up
in any admissible order reaches the top-packed configuration $\{4,2,1,0\}$
with $P=(1)$; two explicit manual removal orders of the corresponding rim
$3$-hooks, namely $$(4,3,2,1)\to(2,2,2,1)\to(1,1,1,1)\to(1)$$ and
$$(4,3,2,1)\to(4,3)\to(2,2)\to(1),$$ reach the same partition, and no $3$-hook
remains at the end
([[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]],
[[thm-e-quotient-controls-hooks-divisible-by-e]]). The size count
$10-1=9=3\cdot3$ exhibits the weight $w_3((4,3,2,1))=3$
([[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

No choice principle is used.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $e=3$, the partition $\lambda=(4,3,2,1)$ of $10$ with the
$\beta$-set $X=X_\lambda=\{7,5,3,1\}$, and $3$-abacus positions $3a+i$ on
runner $i$ at row $a$
([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]).

[F1] For a $\beta$-set $\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\}$ the partition is
$P(\{h_1>\cdots>h_m\})=(h_1-(m-1),\dots,h_m-0)$ with trailing zeros deleted,
and the elements of $X_\lambda$ are the first-column hook lengths of $\lambda$
([[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]]).

[F2] The hooks of a partition with $\beta$-set $Y$ correspond bijectively to
the bead-gap pairs $(b,g)$ of $Y$, i.e. $b\in Y$, $g\notin Y$, $0\le g<b$, the
hook having length $b-g$; it has length divisible by $3$ exactly when
$b\equiv g\pmod3$, and removing it replaces $Y$ by
$(Y\setminus\{b\})\cup\{g\}$, which is again a $\beta$-set, of the partition
obtained by deleting the corresponding rim hook of size $b-g$
([[lem-hooks-are-bead-gap-pairs-on-an-abacus]]).

[F3] A removable border strip of size $3$ is a removable $3$-strip as in
[[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]], and the rim hook attached to the
hook of a node has size the hook length by
[[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]; the $3$-core
$C_3(\lambda)=P(X^{(3)})$ is the top-packed set of the $3$-abacus of a
$\beta$-set of $\lambda$
([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]).

[F4] $C_3(\lambda)$ is the terminal partition of every maximal sequence of
removals of removable border strips of size $3$, and $10=|\lambda|=
|C_3(\lambda)|+3\,w_3(\lambda)$ with $w_3(\lambda)$ the number of such
removals in any maximal sequence
([[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]],
[[prop-core-quotient-size-and-weight-formula]]).

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Beads on the runners: $7=3\cdot2+1$, $5=3\cdot1+2$, $3=3\cdot1+0$, $1=3\cdot0+1$, so the row-label sets are $X^{(3)}_0=\{1\}$ (bead $3$), $X^{(3)}_1=\{2,0\}$ (beads $7,1$) and $X^{(3)}_2=\{1\}$ (bead $5$). Top-packing puts the single beads of runners $0$ and $2$ in row $0$ and the two beads of runner $1$ in rows $0,1$, so $X^{(3)}=\{0\}\cup\{1,4\}\cup\{2\}=\{4,2,1,0\}$ and, listing the four beads in decreasing order, $$C_3(\lambda)=P(X^{(3)})=(4-3,\,2-2,\,1-1,\,0-0)=(1).$$ [given, F1, F3]

2.1 The moves of a single bead one row up are exactly $7\mapsto4$ on runner $1$, $5\mapsto2$ on runner $2$ and $3\mapsto0$ on runner $0$, since $4,2,0\notin X$; each target is a gap on the same runner as its bead, so by [F2] each move removes a rim hook of length $3$. In particular $X^{(3)}$ is reached after exactly these three moves, in any order. [given, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1]

3.1 First removal order: move $7\mapsto4$, then $5\mapsto2$, then $3\mapsto0$, giving the $\beta$-sets $\{7,5,3,1\}\to\{5,4,3,1\}\to\{4,3,2,1\}\to\{4,2,1,0\}$ and, by [F1], the partitions $$(4,3,2,1)\to(2,2,2,1)\to(1,1,1,1)\to(1),$$ each step of size $3$ by [F2] and [F3] and terminating at $C_3(\lambda)=(1)$ by step 1.1. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

3.2 Second removal order: move $3\mapsto0$, then $7\mapsto4$, then $5\mapsto2$, giving $\{7,5,3,1\}\to\{7,5,1,0\}\to\{5,4,1,0\}\to\{4,2,1,0\}$ and the partitions $$(4,3,2,1)\to(4,3)\to(2,2)\to(1),$$ again three steps of size $3$ ending at $(1)$; both orders are maximal, since the terminal configuration $\{4,2,1,0\}$ has no bead with a gap one row above it on its runner, so no rim $3$-hook remains. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The size formula of [F4] reads $10=|C_3(\lambda)|+3\,w_3(\lambda)=1+3\cdot3$, using step 1.1 and the three steps of either order; the partition $(1)$ has the single hook length $1$, so indeed no hook of length $3$ survives, and the two orders agree on the terminal partition as asserted. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 3.2, algebra] ∎

items.title: Equal removable-hook counts do not replace the core test
items.statement:
The number of removable $p$-hooks of a partition determines its $p$-core; in
particular two partitions of $n$ with the same number of removable $p$-hooks
lie in the same $p$-block of the symmetric group.
items.strategy:
## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The prime $p=3$ and the partitions $\lambda=(5)$ and $\mu=(4,1)$ of $5$, with their Young diagrams and hook lengths ([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]).

[F1] For a node $(i,j)$ of $[\nu]$, its hook length is $h_{i,j}(\nu)=\nu_i-j+\nu'_j-i+1$ ([[def-hook-arm-leg-and-hook-length]]). A removable rim strip is a nonempty edge-connected skew diagram containing no $2\times2$ block whose deletion leaves a partition ([[def-removable-border-strip-and-height]]). Node hooks correspond bijectively to removable rim strips, preserving size; hence the number of removable $p$-strips equals the number of node hooks of length $p$ ([[lem-hooks-correspond-to-removable-border-strips]]).

[F2] $e$-core and abacus: for a $\beta$-set $X$ of $\nu$ the top-packed set $X^{(e)}$ is obtained by sliding every bead up as far as possible on its own runner, $C_e(\nu)=P(X^{(e)})$, and $C_e(\nu)$ is the terminal partition of every maximal sequence of removals of removable border strips of size $e$; a partition is an $e$-core exactly when it has no hook of length $e$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[def-beta-set-and-e-runner-abacus-of-a-partition]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]).

[F3] Nakayama: two Specht modules of $k[S_n]$ over a splitting field $k$ of characteristic $p$ lie in the same block if and only if their labels have the same $p$-core ([[thm-nakayama-block-classification-for-symmetric-groups]]).

## Counterexample

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The partition $(5)$. Its hook-length diagram is the single row $5,4,3,2,1$, so by [F1] the unique hook of length $3$ is $H_{1,3}(5)$, a horizontal rim hook of size $3$ spanning the nodes $(1,3),(1,4),(1,5)$ whose removal leaves the partition $(2)$; hence $(5)$ has exactly one removable $3$-hook. Its $\beta$-set is $X_\lambda=\{b_1\}=\{5\}$, a single bead on runner $2$ at row $1$; top-packing slides it to row $0$, so $X^{(3)}=\{2\}$ and $C_3((5))=P(\{2\})=(2)$, a $3$-core since $2<3$ and $(2)$ has hook lengths $2,1$. [given, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 The partition $(4,1)$. Its hook-length diagram is $5,3,2,1$ in the first row and $1$ in the second, so by [F1] the unique hook of length $3$ is $H_{1,2}(4,1)$, whose rim hook is the horizontal strip $(1,2),(1,3),(1,4)$ with complement $(1,1)$; hence $(4,1)$ also has exactly one removable $3$-hook. Its $\beta$-set is $X_\mu=\{b_1,b_2\}=\{5,1\}$, with $5$ on runner $2$ at row $1$ and $1$ on runner $1$ at row $0$; top-packing slides the bead $5$ to the position $2$, so $X^{(3)}=\{2,1\}$ and $C_3((4,1))=P(\{2,1\})=(1,1)$, a $3$-core since $(1,1)$ has hook lengths $2,1$. [given, F1, F2, construct]

2.1 The two partitions therefore have the same number (one) of removable $3$-hooks, but their $3$-cores are the distinct partitions $(2)$ and $(1,1)$ of size $2$; by [F3] the Specht modules $S^{(5)}_k$ and $S^{(4,1)}_k$ lie in different blocks of $k[S_5]$ for every splitting field $k$ of characteristic $3$. The top-packed abacus test of [F2] distinguishes the two configurations (one bead on runner $2$ versus beads on runners $2$ and $1$), while the local removable-hook count does not, so no such count can replace the core test. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 1.2] ∎

Both partitions have $3$-weight $1$, so even the weight may agree while the blocks differ; the invariant that separates them is the runner distribution of the beads, not the number of removable hooks.

items.title: The complete weight-one decomposition matrix for S3 at p=3

Take $e=p=3$ and the weight-one configuration $n=3$, $\gamma=\varnothing$ of [[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]; the three partitions of $3$ with $3$-core $\varnothing$ are $\lambda_1=(3)\rhd\lambda_2=(2,1)\rhd\lambda_3=(1,1,1)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). The associated q-Schur weight-one class over a field $F$ of characteristic $3$ with $q=1$ and $d\ge3$ has the complete Weyl/simple decomposition matrix, with rows and columns in the order $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3$, equal to $$\begin{pmatrix}1&1&0\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}.$$ Applying the Schur functor and the conjugation/duality dictionary gives the Murphy Specht rows $[S^{\lambda_1}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_2}_{\mathrm M}]+[D^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]$, $[S^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]=[D^{\lambda_3}_{\mathrm M}]$, which in the page's $3$-regular labels $(3),(2,1)$ is the matrix $$\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$$ with rows $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ ([[thm-nakayama-block-classification-for-symmetric-groups]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]); the group-side entries are verified directly from the two-dimensional model $S^{(2,1)}$ of characteristic $3$, whose all-ones vector spans a trivial submodule with sign quotient, together with $S^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$ and $S^{(1,1,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$.

No choice principle is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The prime $p=e=3$, the partitions $(3)$, $(2,1)$, $(1,1,1)$ of $n=3$, and the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F$ of $S_F(d,3)$ for $d\ge3$ over any field $F$ of characteristic $3$, with $q=1$ and quantum characteristic $e=3$ (for example $F=\mathbb F_3$).

[F1] $3$-cores: the $3$-core of a partition is computed by removing rim $3$-hooks until none remains; $C_3((3))=\varnothing$, $C_3((2,1))=\varnothing$, $C_3((1,1,1))=\varnothing$, and these are all the partitions of $3$ with core $\varnothing$, ordered by dominance as $(3)\rhd(2,1)\rhd(1,1,1)$ ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]], [[thm-e-core-is-independent-of-the-rim-hook-removal-order]]).

[F2] The balanced positive Jantzen-submodule formula is [[thm-q-schaper-virtual-radical-layer-formula]] and its beta signs are [[def-alternating-weyl-and-specht-symbols-from-beta-sequences]]. Every Weyl module has its nonzero norm-one simple head and $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$, with absolute simple heads and base-change-compatible forms ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]). The specific three-row computation is proved below.

[F3] The exact integral Schur corner/form/radical identity is [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]], steps 1.1–5.1. The specific Murphy forms/actions are computed locally from the independent integral Murphy datum and row action ([[lem-dj-bridge-murphy-cellular-basis-and-cell-form]], [[lem-dj-bridge-row-permutation-module-standard-action]]). The signed conjugate module/form identity is [[thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell]]. No universal finite-$e$ restricted nonzero criterion is used.

[F4] Group side: the simple $k[S_3]$-modules at $p=3$ are $D^{(3)}$ and $D^{(2,1)}$, indexed by the $3$-regular partitions $(3),(2,1)$ ([[thm-nakayama-block-classification-for-symmetric-groups]], [[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]).

[F5] Tabloid model: the permutation module $M^{(2,1)}_k$ over a field $k$ has the three tabloids $v_1,v_2,v_3$ as a basis, where $v_i$ is the tabloid whose singleton second row is $\{i\}$, and $\sigma\cdot v_i=v_{\sigma(i)}$; the Specht module $S^{(2,1)}_k\subseteq M^{(2,1)}_k$ has basis $e_t=v_3-v_1$ and $e_u=v_2-v_1$. Moreover $S^{(3)}_k$ is the trivial module and $S^{(1,1,1)}_k$ is the sign module The characteristic-$3$ constructions use [[def-integral-specht-lattice-and-base-change]]; their basis and actions are verified in step 4.1. The James form quotient is [[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]].

## Verification

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 The labels and their cores. The hook-length diagrams of the three partitions of $3$ are $3,2,1$ for $(3)$; $3,1$ in the first row and $1$ in the second for $(2,1)$; and $3,2,1$ vertically for $(1,1,1)$. In each case there is exactly one hook of length $3$ and removing its rim hook leaves the empty partition, so all three partitions have $3$-core $\varnothing$; conversely any partition of $3$ with core $\varnothing$ is one of these, since a partition whose core has size $3$ is its own core, and $\varnothing$ has size $0=3-3$. Dominance orders them as $(3)\rhd(2,1)\rhd(1,1,1)$. [given, F1]

2.1 Compute the Weyl matrix directly. First work over $\mathbb F_3$ with lift $R=\mathbb Z_{(3)}$, $\hat q=1$, so the only nonzero hook valuation at rank three is $v([3]_1)=1$. The conjugate beta sequence of $(3)$ is $(3,2,1)$. Its hook pairs $(3,2)$ and $(3,1)$ give the balanced sequences $(5,0,1)$ and $(4,2,0)$, of sorted shapes $(1,1,1)$ with sign $-1$ and $(2,1)$ with sign $+1$, respectively. The other pair has coefficient zero. Thus its positive sum is $[W^{(2,1)}]-[W^{(1,1,1)}]$. For $(2,1)$, beta $(4,2,0)$ and its only nonzero pair $(3,1)$ give $(5,1,0)$, shape $(1,1,1)$ with sign $+1$, so its positive sum is $[W^{(1,1,1)}]$. The column shape has no row pair and zero positive sum, hence $W^{(1,1,1)}=L^{(1,1,1)}$. Positivity and $W(1)=\operatorname{rad}W$ then show that $W^{(2,1)}(1)=L^{(1,1,1)}$ and every higher submodule is zero, giving $[W^{(2,1)}]=[L^{(2,1)}]+[L^{(1,1,1)}]$. Substitute into the first sum to get $[L^{(2,1)}]$; the same argument gives $[W^{(3)}]=[L^{(3)}]+[L^{(2,1)}]$. This proves exactly the displayed complete Weyl matrix. Scalar extension to any original field $F$ of characteristic three preserves the Weyl modules/forms and the composition series, since all Schur simple heads are absolutely simple by [F2]. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Determine the specific corner images directly. The group row symmetrizer $x_{(3)}=\sum_{w\in S_3}w$ satisfies $x_{(3)}^2=6x_{(3)}$, so its rank-one Murphy form is zero in characteristic three. In the rank-one column cell the generator is $1$ and its square coefficient is $1$; the higher ideal contains $1+T_1$ and $1+T_2$ (the latter is a conjugate of the former), so this cell and its nonzero form quotient are the sign module. For the middle cell put $x=1+T_1$, $c_0=x$ and $c_1=xT_2$ modulo the higher row ideal. Its row symmetrizer satisfies $x_{(3)}=x+xT_2+xT_2T_1$, so $c_1T_1=-c_0-c_1$ while $c_0T_1=c_0$; and $T_2^2=1$ gives $c_0T_2=c_1$, $c_1T_2=c_0$. Thus its generator matrices are $M_1=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\-1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $M_2=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. The independent cell products $x^2=2x$, $xT_2x=x_{(3)}-x\equiv-x$ and $xT_2^2x=2x$ give $G=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&-1\\-1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&2\\2&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ over $F$. Its radical is the line $(1,-1)$; modulo it both generators act by $1$, so $D_{\mathrm M}^{(2,1)}$ is the nonzero trivial module. These two simple images are distinct since $1\ne-1$. The exact corner/form identity [F3] therefore kills precisely $L^{(3)}$ among the three labels. Projecting the Weyl matrix just proved gives all displayed Murphy Specht rows over the original $F$, without any general finite-$e$ nonzero-label criterion. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Dipper-James rows and the direct group computation. Conjugating the partitions $(3)\leftrightarrow(1,1,1)$, $(2,1)\leftrightarrow(2,1)$ and applying the signed $\theta$-pullback to every Hecke module, the rows of step 3.1 become $[S^{(1,1,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]$, $[S^{(2,1)}]=[D^{(2,1)}]+[D^{(3)}]$ and $[S^{(3)}]=[D^{(3)}]$ in the $3$-regular labels, that is, the matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ with rows $(3),(2,1),(1,1,1)$ and columns $(3),(2,1)$. For the independent direct check, construct the tabloid module over $k$ using [F5]. Every middle-shape polytabloid is a difference $v_i-v_j$, and these span the two independent vectors $e_t,e_u$ displayed in [F5], so they are a basis of $S^{(2,1)}_k$. A one-row polytabloid is its unique tabloid, giving the trivial module; a one-column polytabloid is the nonzero alternating sum of all six distinct tabloids, giving the sign module. Put $w:=e_t+e_u=v_3-v_1+v_2-v_1=v_1+v_2+v_3$ in characteristic $3$: then $w\ne0$ spans a one-dimensional submodule, since $\sigma\cdot v_i=v_{\sigma(i)}$ gives $\sigma\cdot w=w$ for every $\sigma\in S_3$, so it realises the trivial module; and in the quotient, $(12)\cdot e_t+e_t=(v_3-v_2)+(v_3-v_1)=2v_3-v_1-v_2=3v_3-w\equiv0$ shows that $(12)$ acts by $-1$. All transpositions are conjugate and act on a one-dimensional quotient, so they all act by $-1$ and the quotient is sign. The orthonormal tabloid form has middle Gram matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ in $(e_t,e_u)$; its characteristic-three kernel is $k(e_t+e_u)=kw$. Thus the James quotient $D^{(2,1)}$ is precisely this sign quotient, while the row form has norm $1$ and $D^{(3)}$ is trivial. With $S^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $S^{(1,1,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ by [F5], and the just-computed $D^{(3)}=\operatorname{triv}$, $D^{(2,1)}=\operatorname{sgn}$ (the complete list is [F4]), the direct rows of $S^{(3)},S^{(2,1)},S^{(1,1,1)}$ are $(1,0),(1,1),(0,1)$, matching the matrix obtained from the Schur functor entry by entry. [F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎
